Compare the additive conductivity from the separated calculations with the measured total conductivity.
measurements: Temperature-dependent thermal conductivity (low to high temperature)
Phonon dispersion curves (e.g., via inelastic neutron scattering)
Electron relaxation time measurements (using THz spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predictive approach yields total conductivity errors consistently above ±30% or fails to capture the crossover between lattice-dominated (below 200 K) and electronic-dominated (above 300 K) behavior, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding that incorporating lattice distortions through relaxation time measurements (PMC11136967::web::010) significantly improves prediction accuracy and on Debye model insights regarding low-temperature acoustic mode contribution.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes a fully decoupled computational scheme to explicitly compute separate lattice (phonon) and electronic thermal transport contributions, rather than blending them, thereby addressing the challenge of conflation in prior analytical models.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Nanostructuring HfNbTaTiZr into controlled nanograin boundary architectures can be used to selectively scatter phonons but have minimal impact on the free-electron transport, and the new predictive approach can accurately capture this differential effect.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr alloy in a bulk single-phase state with large (≫100 nm) grain size.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a processing step via rapid solidification or severe plastic deformation to refine the grain size to an average of ~30–50 nm while keeping the composition and phase unchanged.
hypotheses.conditions: Test samples prepared with both coarse-grained and nanograined microstructures, measured over the temperature range of 300 to 1200 K.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Nanograin boundaries that act as phonon scattering centers without introducing significant electron scattering; the crystallographic phase remains BCC.
hypotheses.mechanism: The refined grain boundaries will significantly reduce lattice thermal conductivity owing to enhanced phonon scattering at grain boundaries (as predicted by classical phonon-boundary scattering theories and analogies from wear-resistant thin films where grain size effects were ruled out to be negligible; PMC11136967::web::013 gives composition effects dominating, so here isolating grain boundary effects). In contrast, electron transport, which often involves longer mean free paths, will be less sensitive to these boundaries. The predictive approach will incorporate a grain boundary scattering term into the phonon Boltzmann transport calculation while leaving the electronic Drude parameters nearly unaltered.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: For nanograined HfNbTaTiZr, a reduction in lattice thermal conductivity by roughly 30–40% relative to coarse-grained samples is expected, leading to a lower overall thermal conductivity prediction by the new model. Concurrent electrical conductivity values will remain almost unchanged.
hypotheses.baseline: The current best models do not adequately account for microstructural modulation of phonon transport in perfect crystals.
hypotheses.boundary: The hypothesis is valid for samples where the grain size reduction does not lead to secondary phase precipitation or excessive electron scattering; extreme nanostructuring (grain sizes below ~20 nm) might begin to affect electrons adversely.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact percentage drop in lattice conductivity is sensitive to the grain boundary quality and distribution. There is some uncertainty in quantifying phonon-boundary scattering effects in complex HEAs.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Incorporating controlled oxygen doping (up to 1 wt.%) into HfNbTaTiZr will selectively influence electron scattering without substantially altering the lattice (phonon) contribution, and the new predictive approach will accurately predict a distinct crossover in dominant heat transport mechanism between low- and high-temperature regimes.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: High-purity, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with negligible oxygen content.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a controlled amount (approx. 1 wt.%) of oxygen into the alloy during processing by reactive melting or controlled oxide addition, ensuring uniform distribution.
hypotheses.conditions: Perform tests on both oxygen-free and oxygen-doped samples over a wide temperature range: below 200 K (where lattice and electronic contributions compete) and between 300 to 1200 K.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Uniform oxygen incorporation that preferentially creates additional electron scattering centers, possibly by distorting local electron density, while the overall BCC structure remains intact.
hypotheses.mechanism: Oxygen doping is expected to increase electron scattering (lowering the electronic contribution to thermal conductivity via reduced relaxation times) as observed in other refractory HEAs (see PMC11136967::web::008 and ::web::017 for conduction trends related to composition). At low temperatures, where phonons dominate, the impact of oxygen is minimal; however, at high temperatures the increased electron scattering will reduce the electronic contribution, leading to an altered total thermal conductivity. The predictive approach will model the oxygen-induced change in free-electron density and relaxation time explicitly, thereby decoupling the changes in the two transport channels.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The oxygen-doped sample will show a decrease in electronic thermal conductivity by an estimated 20–30% relative to the oxygen-free alloy at high temperatures (300–1200 K), with the total conductivity falling into the lower end of the previously measured 10–17 W/(K·m) range. At temperatures below 200 K the conduction contributions should converge with those of the oxygen-free sample.
hypotheses.baseline: Existing analytical formulations tend to mix lattice and electronic contributions and cannot capture oxygen’s selective role on electron transport in HEAs.
hypotheses.boundary: This hypothesis applies only if oxygen is uniformly incorporated at controlled levels (~1 wt.%) without causing phase segregation or formation of second phases. Excess oxygen or inhomogeneous doping would lead to different behavior.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise quantitative change in electronic conductivity due to oxygen doping is not fully established in literature and could vary with processing conditions; the predicted 20–30% reduction is an estimate based on analogous observations in similar refractory HEAs.

Developed and compared three simulation methods (Method 1: linear combination, Method 2: incorporating plasma frequency, and Method 3: including relaxation time measured by THz-TDS) to predict low-frequency electrical conductivity.

Measured and analyzed DC conductivity, frequency-dependent conductivity, XRD (for phase structure and grain size), TEM/SEM (for morphology and uniform elemental distribution), and C-AFM (for surface current mapping).
Conducted mechanical testing (nanoscratch, hardness, corrosion tests) to demonstrate high hardness, excellent wear resistance, and superior corrosion behavior of the films.

Established that compositional modulation (the “cocktail effect”) drives conductivity trends, while grain size differences (around 15–17 nm) have minimal impact on the intrinsic electrical properties.
paper_reported: The Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 film exhibits lower resistivity (down to ~37 μΩ-cm at 1200 nm) compared to the equimolar or Ta+W–dominated compositions.
Including plasma frequency and relaxation time (via THz-TDS) in the conduction models (Methods 2 and 3) considerably improves predictive accuracy over the simple linear combination approach.
A robust linear correlation exists between the composition-weighted (cocktail effect) resistivity predictions and the experimental measurements.

The HEA films show not only favorable electrical properties but also excellent mechanical properties (high hardness, robust corrosion resistance, and promising wear performance for coating applications).
paper_proposed: Exploitation of the cocktail effect to design HEAs that simultaneously deliver high conductivity and good wear resistance.
Application of Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 thin films as coatings for atomic force microscopy (AFM) probe tips to achieve enhanced wear resistance and improved imaging resolution.
Further refinement and validation of conduction models for HEAs, concentrating on the interplay of lattice distortions, plasma frequency variations, and relaxation time effects.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A new predictive model that decouples lattice thermal conductivity from electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr by explicitly accounting for the role of trace oxygen impurities in modifying electron transport while leaving phonon dynamics dominated by intrinsic force‐constant disorder.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr produced using standard processing routes that result in ~1 wt.% oxygen, with a nearly fully dense, defect‐free bulk microstructure.
hypotheses.intervention: Prepare controlled samples of HfNbTaTiZr with significantly reduced oxygen content (e.g., <0.1 wt.% oxygen) using improved melting/high-purity environments, and use the new predictive approach to simulate the lattice thermal conductivity separately from the electronic contribution.
hypotheses.conditions: Test over two temperature regimes: below 200 K where experimental data indicate comparable lattice and electronic contributions, and at high temperatures (300–1200 K) where total measurements are available; same geometric sample dimensions and phase purity must be maintained.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Force-constant fluctuations intrinsic to the HfNbTaTiZr matrix dominate phonon scattering, while oxygen impurities act as electron scattering centers but do not significantly alter the phonon dispersion.
hypotheses.mechanism: The model builds on the observation (in FeCoCrMnNi) that strong force-constant disorder, rather than mass fluctuations, controls phonon lifetimes. By minimizing oxygen concentration, the electronic conductivity is improved and rendered more distinct from the lattice component. The decoupling thereby allows predictions of the lattice transport channel based on anisotropic phonon broadening and Debye-like acoustic behavior. This separation produces an explicit lattice thermal conductivity estimate that is less convoluted with the electronic part, making it more predictive compared to previous approaches that assumed perfect crystals with unfettered electronic-lattice mixing.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The new predictive approach should forecast a lattice thermal conductivity in oxygen-lean HfNbTaTiZr that is roughly 20–30% higher than the lattice contribution extracted from oxygen-containing specimens, with a clear temperature independence below 200 K and a moderate increase at high temperatures. The predicted improvement is in clarity and separation of conduction channels rather than a dramatic numeric shift.
hypotheses.baseline: Earlier analytical methods assumed defect-free perfect crystals and combined all transport channels, leading to ambiguous Debye temperatures and conflated lattice and electronic thermal conductivities.
hypotheses.boundary: Applicable for fully dense bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with controlled oxygen levels; temperature applicability from 15 K to 1200 K, with special emphasis below 200 K for isolating lattice transport.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Exact percent improvement in isolated lattice conductivity may vary with the degree of oxygen reduction and sample purity. Quantification beyond ~20–30% improvement is approximate.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A new predictive approach can independently quantify mode-specific phonon lifetimes in HfNbTaTiZr by incorporating anisotropic force‐constant disorder effects, leading to a prediction of directional lattice thermal conductivity that remains decoupled from electronic contributions.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr in a single-phase polycrystalline state with nominal composition and controlled microstructural homogeneity, similar to high-purity alloys without additional impurities.
hypotheses.intervention: Employ directional inelastic scattering techniques (e.g., inelastic X-ray or neutron scattering) to obtain mode-resolved phonon dispersion and linewidth data from well-textured samples; integrate these experimental inputs into the new predictive model to resolve anisotropic phonon scattering contributions.
hypotheses.conditions: Measure and simulate the phonon properties along at least two high-symmetry directions over a temperature range spanning below 200 K (where electron contribution is minimal) and above 300 K, ensuring the measurement resolution is sufficient to resolve anisotropic linewidth variations.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The anisotropy in the phonon dispersion and scattering rates—observed as different power-law behaviors (e.g., (ℏω)^4.5 at low energies and (ℏω)^1.7 at higher energies in some directions in FeCoCrMnNi)—serves as a key mediator that distinguishes the lattice conduction paths.
hypotheses.mechanism: By decomposing the phonon spectrum into polarization and directional components, the model can isolate those phonons that carry heat effectively. Building on the observation from FeCoCrMnNi that the acoustic regime persists throughout the Brillouin zone despite strong disorder (PMC9726824, sections on phonon dispersions and broadening), the approach applies a similar analysis to HfNbTaTiZr. It predicts that the longitudinal modes, with their specific scattering regimes, largely determine the lattice thermal conductivity. Since these phonon characteristics are only weakly influenced by electronic carriers, the model can separately forecast them.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The model should predict distinct lattice thermal conductivity contributions along different crystallographic directions; for example, one may expect a modest anisotropy (potentially on the order of 10–20%) in the lattice conductivity values. At low temperatures (<200 K) the lattice conductivity should be nearly constant, with the longitudinal phonon modes clearly dominating the transport.
hypotheses.baseline: Earlier approaches provided bulk averaged estimates that assumed perfect crystals and did not resolve the anisotropic phonon dynamics, leading to conflated or averaged Debye parameters.
hypotheses.boundary: Applicable to well-textured or oriented HfNbTaTiZr samples; valid over a temperature range where phonon properties dominate (<200 K) and can be extended to high temperatures with proper electronic subtraction.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Quantitative predictions of the anisotropy magnitude are approximate due to limited available data on mode-dependent phonon lifetimes in refractory HEAs. The 10–20% anisotropy is an estimate.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A predictive approach that incorporates grain boundary engineering as a tunable parameter can separate the contributions of phonon scattering from intrinsic force‐constant disorder and extrinsic boundary scattering in HfNbTaTiZr, leading to improved decoupling of lattice from electronic thermal transport.

hypotheses.intervention: Process HfNbTaTiZr using field-assisted sintering or severe plastic deformation to refine the grain size to the nanocrystalline regime (e.g., grain sizes below 100 nm) without significantly altering the elemental composition; then deploy the new predictive model with explicit treatment of grain boundary scattering.

hypotheses.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries introduce additional phonon scattering sites that reduce the lattice contribution; however, if properly modeled, they provide a handle to distinctively tune the lattice thermal conductivity independent of the electronic component.
hypotheses.mechanism: The new predictive approach integrates traditional phonon scattering mechanisms (due to force-constant disorder) with additional boundary scattering terms (using, for example, a modified Callaway model). In nanocrystalline samples, enhanced grain boundary scattering will significantly reduce the phonon mean free paths without affecting electronic transport markedly, thus accentuating the separation between lattice and electronic contributions. This concept is inspired by similar effects observed in other refractory alloys and builds on the idea that defect density can tune phonon transport independently.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: For nanocrystalline HfNbTaTiZr, the lattice thermal conductivity is predicted to be reduced by approximately 30% relative to coarse-grained samples, with the decoupling of the electronic contribution remaining evident (e.g., a clear difference in temperature trends between lattice and electronic channels). The model thereby outperforms earlier approaches by providing a quantitative prediction that accounts for grain size as a controllable parameter.
hypotheses.baseline: Previous simulations assumed defect-free, bulk crystals where grain boundary scattering was absent, leading to oversimplified predictions that conflated intrinsic lattice and electronic heat conduction.
hypotheses.boundary: The approach is applicable for samples with well-controlled grain sizes ranging from nanocrystalline (<100 nm) to coarse-grained (>1 µm) within the HfNbTaTiZr system and for temperatures where grain boundary scattering remains effective (typically at lower and intermediate temperatures, though high-temperature behavior necessitates electronic correction).
hypotheses.uncertainty: The estimated 30% reduction is approximate; actual grain boundary effects may be influenced by boundary structure and possible impurity segregation, and there is uncertainty in separating their contribution from intrinsic phonon scattering.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A new predictive approach based on MD simulation with a rigorous separation of phonon dynamics will predict that the lattice thermal conductivity (kₚ) for HfNbTaTiZr follows a power‐law decrease with temperature, with an exponent close to –0.45 over 300–1200 K, outperforming earlier Debye‐temperature based estimates.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: High-purity, defect‐minimized bulk HfNbTaTiZr in the refractory high-entropy alloy state.
hypotheses.intervention: Application of an MD-based predictive scheme that isolates the lattice (phonon) contribution by using an interatomic potential validated for refractory systems, decoupled from free electron models.
hypotheses.conditions: Temperature range from 300 K to 1200 K; samples with minimal impurity (oxygen less than 1 wt.%); defect-free microstructure.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Intrinsic atomic-scale anharmonicity and chemical disorder controlling phonon scattering.
hypotheses.mechanism: The approach calculates phonon trajectories and their scattering rates directly via MD, yielding a power-law relationship (kₚ ∼ T^(–n)) that inherently captures the complex anharmonic interactions present in the disordered refractory alloy. This avoids conflating lattice and electronic contributions by excluding free-electron thermal transport in the simulation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The lattice thermal conductivity will decrease with temperature following kₚ ∼ T^(–0.45) (within ±0.05 uncertainty on the exponent) and yield estimates 30–40% more accurate than classical analytical predictions when compared with experimental lattice-only measurements.
hypotheses.baseline: Earlier calculations based on Debye-temperature estimates or semi-empirical models that mix the two contributions.
hypotheses.boundary: Valid for bulk, compositionally homogeneous, defect-minimized HfNbTaTiZr samples within the tested temperature range; not applicable when extrinsic scattering (e.g., high impurity or nano-structuring) dominates.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise exponent may vary slightly due to the mass and bonding differences in refractory elements relative to previously simulated HEAs; uncertainty in the interatomic potential accuracy remains.

hypotheses.structural_mediator: Enhanced scattering at engineered grain boundaries which predominantly affect the mean free path of free electrons over phonons.
hypotheses.mechanism: According to the modeling, grain boundaries introduce additional scattering centers that lower the mobility of free electrons (owing to their long MFP in refractory metals) while phonon transport, especially for the dominant low-frequency modes in a disordered lattice, is less perturbed. This selective scattering leads to a relative reduction in electronic thermal conductivity without significantly affecting lattice conductivity.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Total measured thermal conductivity will show a temperature-dependent crossover: at low temperatures (<200 K), electron conduction is substantially reduced (by ~40%), making the lattice contribution more apparent; overall conductivity reduction of roughly 15–25% compared to non-engineered samples is expected.
hypotheses.baseline: Standard, coarse-grained HfNbTaTiZr samples where electron and lattice contributions are not separated via microstructural control.
hypotheses.boundary: Applicable for samples where grain boundary density can be precisely controlled and when the variability in electronic conduction dominates over other scattering mechanisms; not applicable if grain boundaries induce secondary phases or if impurity scattering predominates.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The degree of electron vs phonon scattering at nano-scale grain boundaries in a refractory HEA is not well established, therefore the quantitative suppression (40% for electrons, 10% for phonons) has uncertainty and requires experimental calibration.

Other routes such as CIP followed by sintering/HIP and swaging produced samples with higher residual porosity, increased oxygen content, chemical inhomogeneities, and notably lower or variable hardness, sometimes accompanied by cracking or phase separation.

paper_proposed: Future work suggested further investigating processing methods (e.g., optimized hot forging or swaging conditions) to fully eliminate residual porosity in larger specimens.

paper_did: Prepared and characterized the RM(Nb)IC alloy NV2 (nominal Nb–30Ti–10Si–2Al–5Cr–3Fe–5Sn–2Hf) in as‐cast and heat‐treated states using high‐purity elements and controlled melting/heat‐treatment processes.

Performed phase identification and microstructural analysis by XRD and EPMA to document the presence of phases such as Nb solid solution (Nbss), A15–Nb3X, various Nb5Si3 silicides, Nb3Si (stable and metastable forms) and other phases (e.g., μ and π phases), as well as noting macrosegregation phenomena.

Measured physical properties including density and hardness as well as conducted isothermal oxidation experiments at 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C to obtain mass‐change kinetics, identify oxidation scales, and compare oxidation behavior with other RM(Nb)ICs, RCCAs and RHEAs.
paper_reported: That Fe addition in NV2 stabilizes several phases—including a controlled increase in A15–Nb3X at the expense of Nbss—and reduces pest oxidation at lower temperatures, with clear evidence from oxidation kinetics and oxygen contamination profiles.

Detailed spatial variation of phases (top, bulk, bottom of ingot) and variations in chemical compositions among phases (for example, differences in silicide types and eutectic compositions) were reported.

Quantitative relationships were established between solute concentrations, phase volume fractions, and resultant hardness/oxidation performance, with comparisons made to other alloys in the RM(Nb)IC series as well as RCCAs and RHEAs.
paper_proposed: Future work to optimize alloy design by tailoring the volume fractions and distributions of key phases (such as A15–Nb3X versus Nbss) to further improve oxidation resistance and high‐temperature strength.

Exploration of processing parameters (e.g., heat treatment temperatures and durations) to control macrosegregation, liquation, and the stability of both conventional and complex concentrated/high entropy phases.
Additional studies to correlate solute partitioning and microstructural evolution (including the formation of diffusion zones) with mechanical and oxidation properties under service conditions.
